text: Margaret Bourchier, Countess of Bath (née Donington; c. 1509 – 20 December 1561), was an English Tudor noblewoman known for securing three high-profile and advantageous marriages during her lifetime, as well as for successfully arranging socially significant marriages for many of her children. Through her descendants, she is a common ancestor of numerous English noble families. She was the only daughter and sole heiress of John Donington, a member of the Worshipful Company of Salters, and Elizabeth Pye. Upon her first marriage to Sir Thomas Kitson, a wealthy merchant and Sheriff of London, she became the owner of Hengrave Hall in Suffolk, where she installed a tomb and stained glass window commemorating her three husbands, all of whom predeceased her. She is buried in Hengrave Church. The marriage to Sir Thomas Kitson produced five children. Her second marriage, to courtier Sir Richard Long, occurred in 1540, shortly after the death of her first husband, and they had four children. Her final marriage was to John Bourchier, 2nd Earl of Bath, on 11 December 1548, after which she was styled Countess of Bath. Prior to this marriage, she insisted that her son-in-law, Lord FitzWarin, marry her daughter Frances Kitson. The marriage settlement guaranteed Margaret retained control over her property. The Earl and Countess of Bath made Hengrave Hall their primary residence. The couple had two daughters.
